brief.topic: Why airport signs work when nobody has time to read: practical wayfinding principles for rushed interfaces
brief.desiredChange: Apply six airport-wayfinding principles and a pre-ship glance test to make rushed interfaces easier to scan, act on, and trust.

slides.title: Why airport signs work when nobody has time to read
slides.purpose: Open with the promise that rushed interfaces should work at a glance without sacrificing deeper explanation.
evidence: Familiar conceptual moment: navigating toward a gate while moving
Thesis: design for the glance, then reward the read
slides.focalArtifact: The title thesis expressed as a destination-and-direction statement

slides.title: Nobody arrives at the sign calm
slides.purpose: Establish the divided-attention conditions that define rushed use.
evidence: Conceptual traveler state: moving, uncertain, interrupted, and carrying a goal
No quantitative or empirical claim
slides.focalArtifact: A traveler-state inventory centered on the unresolved goal

slides.title: Rushed is not the same as simple
slides.purpose: Show that limited attention and task complexity coexist, so clarity requires structure rather than mere subtraction.
evidence: Four simultaneous needs: orient, choose, act, and confirm
Conceptual contrast between less information and better-sequenced information
slides.focalArtifact: The four needs that remain even when reading time collapses

slides.title: 1 — Announce destination before detail
slides.purpose: Teach teams to lead with the user’s goal rather than procedure or system language.
evidence: Conceptual destination-first sign
Hypothetical procedure-first interface prompt
slides.focalArtifact: A destination-first instruction and its procedure-first counterpart

slides.title: Hierarchy changes with distance
slides.purpose: Explain how information priority changes as a user approaches, chooses, and pauses.
evidence: Three conceptual horizons: decide from afar, confirm at the choice, read detail when stopped
No claim about a named airport or formal signage standard
slides.focalArtifact: The three information horizons along one journey

slides.title: 2 — One decision at each decision point
slides.purpose: Show that each moment should answer the choice the user must make now, not every later choice.
evidence: Conceptual corridor junction
Hypothetical multi-step product flow with premature decisions removed
slides.focalArtifact: A current fork separated from future forks

slides.title: 3 — Reveal detail in sequence
slides.purpose: Reframe progressive disclosure as a deliberate route through questions rather than hidden complexity.
evidence: Question sequence: destination, direction, confirmation, local detail
Each reveal answers the next user question
slides.focalArtifact: A four-stage chain of questions and answers

slides.title: 4 — Consistency beats cleverness
slides.purpose: Argue for a stable vocabulary that users can recognize across repeated decisions.
evidence: Repeated conceptual labels and symbols across decision points
Contrast between recognition and reinterpretation
slides.focalArtifact: A small cue vocabulary repeated across a route

slides.title: 5 — Use redundant cues
slides.purpose: Show how overlapping words, icons, color, position, and shape make instructions resilient.
evidence: One conceptual instruction expressed through multiple cue types
The message remains understandable when one cue is unavailable
slides.focalArtifact: A single instruction with independent reinforcing cues

slides.title: Confirmation is part of navigation
slides.purpose: Teach teams to preserve orientation and reassure users after they act.
evidence: Conceptual continuity marker after a turn
Hypothetical persistent progress after a product action
slides.focalArtifact: A before-action choice connected to an after-action confirmation

slides.title: 6 — Separate scan mode from read mode
slides.purpose: Distinguish glanceable action and status from explanation that belongs where users can pause.
evidence: Conceptual rushed state and safe-to-read state
Primary action and status remain available without parsing prose
slides.focalArtifact: Two attention modes with different information needs

slides.title: Translate the sign into the interface
slides.purpose: Map wayfinding behaviors to familiar product moments without copying airport visual style.
evidence: Conceptual mappings for checkout recovery, incident response, onboarding, and permission prompts
Each mapping uses a principle from the preceding sequence
slides.focalArtifact: Paired wayfinding behaviors and rushed-interface responses

slides.title: Start with the decision map
slides.purpose: Give teams a practical method for structuring a rushed journey before styling screens.
evidence: Four steps: identify the goal, mark decision points, define the attention window, assign cue and confirmation
Method is presented as a practical synthesis, not a formal standard

slides.title: The pre-ship glance test
slides.purpose: Turn the six principles into a compact review that product teams can apply before shipping.
evidence: Six review questions: destination, current decision, sequence, consistency, redundancy, scan/read separation
Questions directly trace to the approved principles

slides.title: Design for the glance. Reward the read.
slides.purpose: Close with a memorable rule that combines immediate clarity with available depth.
evidence: Concise recap of the six principles
Final standard: make the next step unmistakable and deeper explanation available
slides.focalArtifact: The closing rule paired with the next unmistakable step
